newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada general-diplomat to turn hand to Irish arms.
newsitem.headline: Canada general-diplomat to turn hand to Irish arms.

text.p: If Canada's John de Chastelain is named head of a body to disarm guerrillas in Northern Ireland he is likely to find himself drawing heavily on his ample military and diplomatic experience.

Cool under fire and expert at smoothing ruffled feathers, John Gardyne Drummond de Chastelain worked himself up from private to four-star general and Canada's top soldier during 40 years in the military before retiring at the end of 1995.

But he also served during 1993 as Canada's ambassador to the United States, and during his time in the military he had to deal with touchy hot spots, from Cyprus and the Gulf War to a military standoff at home with Canadian Mohawk Indians.
"If anybody could be said to be ideal for the job, he'd be the guy," commented retired Brigadier General Jim Hanson, who worked under de Chastelain.

De Chastelain is already on a three-man commission led by former U.S. Sen. George Mitchell that is trying to bring peace to Northern Ireland, and his name is most often mentioned as a potential head of an arms-decommissioning panel.

Born in Romania on July 30, 1937, to British-American parents who worked for Allied intelligence during the Second World War, he went to boarding school in Scotland and then in 1955 joined the Calgary Highlanders in Canada as a bagpiper.

Hanson suggested he might need his sense of humor and individuality to survive among the hardened parties in the Northern Ireland conflict, where the Irish Republican Army (IRA) is seeking an end to British rule.
De Chastelain still dons a kilt to play the bagpipe or to join Scottish country dancing.

He displayed a delightful sense of bravado in his five years as chief of defense staff -- the top military position -- when he frequently parachuted into Canadian bases as a way of meeting ordinary soldiers and showing who is in charge.

"A lot of people thought I shouldn't have been jumping, that I'd break a leg or something," he recounted four years ago to the Financial Post. "Some people would say, 'How come they let you?' And I'd say, 'Who's they?'"

He did receive a black mark in July from an independent Canadian commission that looked into Canada's botched mission to Somalia, during which peacekeepers shot two unarmed Somalis in the back as they fled, killing one, and tortured to death a teenager.
Those incidents took place when he was ambassador. But the report said he had not put adequate controls in place or ensured the peacekeepers were prepared for deployment.
The soldiers were members of Canada's elite Airborne Regiment, which was eventually disbanded after the killings and after details of foul initiation rituals were revealed.

"General de Chastelain's primary failure may be characterized as one of nonexistent control and indifferent supervision ... that fostered more failings among his subordinates," the commission concluded.
Hanson sought to excuse the general by saying the whole military system tended to function by trusting subordinates.
But he did say of his work in Northern Ireland: "What he'll have to be is extremely cautious, and to see everyting in writing or hand-carved."
De Chastelain himself recognizes the difficulties. He spoke this month about the damage the years of fighting has done to the confidence each side has of the other.

"There is a lack of trust on the part of some of the parties, in particular the Unionist parties (pressing for continued British rule), that Sinn Fein and the IRA are really serious," he told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
